why: Sample drawn only from dog owners, not random from all city residents. D correctly identifies the bias. A over-generalizes from biased sample; B wrongly wants more of the same biased group; C replaces one biased subgroup with another.

Random sample from people who liked the book; generalize only to that group. D correctly scopes to book-likers. A/B over-generalize to all moviegoers or all book readers; C reverses the sampled population (dislike instead of like).

Random 200 residents, 87% satisfied. Neither statement must be true: I treats sample stat as exact population value, II assumes another sample must replicate exactly. A is correct. B fails on population estimate; C fails on sample variability; D fails on both.

Random sample of history professors from CSU system. Largest population = all history professors at all CSUs. C is correct. A/B over-generalize to all US professors; D broadens to all CSU professors, missing the history restriction.

Random 1000 from city, 78% satisfied. None of the three statements must be true. A is correct. B wrongly assumes another sample replicates exactly; C treats sample stat as exact population value and assumes replication; D extends to a different city entirely.

Random baobab trees of a certain age from a habitat, assigned to treatment groups. Largest group = all trees of that age in that habitat. B is correct. A restricts to just the selected trees; C over-generalizes to all of South Africa; D appears similar to B in garbled OCR but likely differs in original.

Surveyed 20 families at a playground — convenience sample biased toward families with children. C correctly identifies the flawed method. A treats biased result as population value; B blames sample size instead of bias; D directly fails to detect the non-representative sampling.

Online poll on cable news show = voluntary response bias, not a random sample. B correctly identifies the non-random sampling. A fixates on percentages not summing to 100; C wrongly expects a 50-50 split; D blames time constraints instead of the sampling method.

Random 35 students from one middle school. Largest group = all students at that school. B is correct. A restricts to just the sample; C over-generalizes to all middle schoolers in the city; D extends even further to all students in the city.

Random teams from all trivia teams in a tournament. Largest population = all teams in the tournament. D is correct. A restricts to high-scoring teams; B restricts to just the sample; C restricts to a practice-hours subgroup of the sample.

Random 40 fourth-graders from one school. Largest population = all fourth-graders at that school. B is correct. A restricts to just the sample; C broadens to all students at the school; D over-generalizes to all fourth-graders in the county.
